nameStory: Wild pink gets its name from its beautiful pink spring flowers that bloom wild in rocky places across the eastern United States. The 'sticky catchfly' nickname comes from the plant's tacky stems that can trap small insects - though this doesn't seem to help with pollination, it might protect the flowers from unwanted crawling visitors who would steal nectar without helping to spread pollen.
description: Wild pink is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms compact cushions of narrow leaves topped with clusters of bright pink flowers in spring. The entire plant typically stays under 8 inches tall and spreads into small mats. Its sticky, hairy stems and leaves give it a somewhat fuzzy appearance, and the five-petaled pink flowers are its most eye-catching feature during the brief spring blooming season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink flowers with five notched petals that form neat clusters at the top of stems - each flower is about half an inch across with a tubular base and the petals often look slightly ragged at the edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, cushion-like mats rarely taller than 8 inches, with multiple flowering stems rising from a dense cluster of basal leaves

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly sticky and fuzzy to the touch, arranged in a dense rosette at the base with smaller leaves up the flowering stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly sticky and hairy stems that may trap small insects - run your finger along one and you'll feel the tackiness and soft fuzz

habitat: Wild pink thrives in dry, rocky places like exposed ledges, sandy soils, and open woodlands with good drainage. In New England, look for it on granite outcrops, rocky slopes, and thin soils where many other plants struggle to grow. It particularly loves sunny to partially shaded spots with acidic, well-draining soil.

seasonality.spring: This is wild pink's moment to shine - bright pink flower clusters appear from April through June, making the plant unmistakable during its blooming period.
seasonality.summer: After flowers fade, the low green cushions of narrow leaves remain visible but much less conspicuous among other vegetation.
seasonality.fall: The plant stays green through early fall before dying back, with seed capsules sometimes still visible from spring's flowers.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring growth begins again.

funFact: Despite being called 'sticky catchfly' and regularly trapping small insects on its gooey stems, wild pink doesn't digest these creatures like carnivorous plants do - the bugs just get stuck and die for no benefit to the plant, making it one of nature's accidental insect traps.
confusionNotes: Wild pink might be confused with other spring pinks, but its extremely low, cushion-like growth habit and sticky stems set it apart from taller members of the pink family. The combination of bright pink flowers and tacky, fuzzy stems is your best identification combo.
contextualKnowledge: The pink family name doesn't refer to flower color - many family members have white or other colored flowers. Instead, 'pink' comes from the fringed petal edges that look like they were cut with pinking shears, the zigzag scissors used in sewing.
compareHints: Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time. Fire pink has similar bright flowers but grows much taller on upright stems, while white campion and bladder campion have white flowers and taller growth. Most other catchflies in New England either bloom later in summer or have much different flower colors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
